headline: US economy showing mixed signals — resilient growth but cooling labour market — while Q2 earnings solid but tech CapEx scrutiny rising
reasoning: Poole describes the US economic backdrop as muddled: Q2 GDP is expected to show resilience and inflation has come off its peaks, but it remains well above target, suggesting some entrenchment. Labour market data is neither weak nor particularly strong. On the earnings side, Q2 results have been solid overall, but the tech sector is generating anxiety because large CapEx commitments are being met with investor concern about the timeline and quantum of returns on that investment.
quote: It's a bit of a muddle at the moment I think, because there's clearly some resilience in the US economy. And Q2 GDP will show that inflation has come off its peaks and that really reflects oil prices. But it's still well above the central defense target. And that is pointing to some inflation that's becoming established. But beyond that, you are still seeing some signs of not necessarily weakness, but not strength in the labor market as well. From an earnings perspective, you've seen some really solid earnings in Q2 so far, although that has come with some angst in itself, particularly around the tech sector where commitments, even more CapEx is being met with concern around the return on that investment.

headline: Bank of Japan window for rate hikes is closing, leaving yen weakness and sticky inflation as structural headwinds over the next 18 months
reasoning: Isaac Poole argues the Bank of Japan has historically been late to act on monetary policy, and the best window to hike rates was in 2025, which they navigated only cautiously. Now, the opportunity for material rate hikes is rapidly closing, which will leave persistent yen weakness that keeps inflation sticky. The Japanese economy is okay but not accelerating, meaning the BoJ faces a difficult backdrop. Over the longer term, these fundamental challenges could weigh on Japan's outlook.
quote: I think the Bank of Japan is going to be the the interesting one this week. Uh, there's no, no real expectation for, for a rate hike. Um, even though we've seen the ongoing weakness in the yen and, and sort of jaw boning around trying to get that to strengthen, historically, the Bank of Japan has been late to the party. Uh, it was probably a really good window in 2025 for the Bank of Japan to hike rates, and they did that very cautiously. Now we're at a point where their window is is perhaps rapidly closing to get material rate hikes in. And I think that's going to be a challenge for their, their um, their economy looking forward over the next 18 months, uh, just being slow to the party will leave some weakness in the yen that's going to keep inflation sticky.

headline: Tech sector credit spreads widening on CapEx return concerns and heavy issuance pipeline, leaving investors cautious
reasoning: Poole highlights that while broad credit spreads have remained relatively tight, the most notable widening has occurred in tech issuance — including investment-grade tech — where more risk is being priced in relative to the broader economy. He flags a large pipeline of further issuance from tech companies ahead. The combination of investor concerns about return on CapEx, equity price volatility, and widening credit spreads in the sector is likely to leave investors cautious for some time.
quote: Credit spreads in general have remained pretty tight. We've seen a little bit of widening, but not a great deal even in high yield space where you've seen the biggest widening has been in that tech issuance. And there you're seeing even investment grade tech spreads widen out. That is, there is more risk being priced in to this sector than the broader economy. And we know that there is going to be even more issuance coming down this year. So that's something I think that sort of interplay between the concerns around return on investment on the CapEx side and volatility in equity prices, and then the increase in spreads you're seeing in this sector, that could be something, I think, that will leave investors cautious for some time to come.

headline: Central banks expected to hold rates as elevated bond yields do some of the heavy lifting on tightening financial conditions
reasoning: Isaac Poole argues that central banks globally will move into a wait-and-see mode given geopolitical-driven oil price volatility and uncertainty around second-round inflation effects. He notes that US 10-year Treasury yields near 4.7% — close to 18-year highs — are already tightening financial conditions by pushing up the cost of capital and making credit markets more expensive. This reduces the urgency for central banks to hike further. His base case is that central banks can hold for the rest of the year and that the front end of the curve has likely peaked, provided inflation does not become more entrenched.
quote: I think that the volatility that you're seeing in the oil prices as a result of geopolitical tensions and just uncertainty around the war in the Middle East is going to leave central banks cautious around oil prices... perhaps less urgency there because you're seeing those US Treasury yields are doing some of the heavy lifting at the moment. Ten year Treasury yields are sitting up around 4.7%. And you look across the world there is very clearly a bias towards yields remaining higher for longer, whether that's in the US or Europe or in Japan, for that matter. All of that is doing some of the heavy lifting for the fed and for other central banks. It's pushing up the cost of capital. It's making some parts of the credit markets a little bit more expensive. And that will slow the economy to some extent.

headline: Ascolum Capital's Isaac Poole sees US Fed under Warsh adopting minimalist, less communicative approach with hawkish hold stance
reasoning: Poole noted the Fed statement under new chair Warsh contained far less communication than usual, a trend likely to continue. The statement was relatively hawkish, with focus shifting toward inflation stability over the labor market mandate. Around half of Fed members saw risk of a rate hike this year. Poole expects markets will need to adjust to less forward guidance, potentially refocusing on the real economy rather than guessing Fed reactions. He sees the Fed as indicating policy will remain relatively unchanged unless dragged toward a hike.
quote: What was communicated was relatively hawkish. I think the focus in on getting inflation stability over the labor market mandate that the Fed has was interesting to note, as was the dot plots where around half of the members saw the risk of a hike this year. And of course, we had one conspicuous dot missing from Fed Chair Wash. And again, that probably points to the fact that these dots are going to change over time. We won't have them represented in the same way every quarter that we do now. And that means markets are going to have to get used to a different type of communication style.

headline: Ascolum Capital strongly favours fixed income with multi-decade high yields offering attractive income and downside protection
reasoning: Poole makes a strong case for fixed income in the current environment, noting that yields on Australian government bonds, US Treasuries and other developed market government bonds are at multi-decade highs that many investors in their working career have never seen before. He says high-quality credit yields are also very attractive as a result. He recommends remaining well exposed to fixed income for yield and downside protection as part of a diversified 60/40-style portfolio.
quote: If you think about a sort of traditional 6040 in that 40 percent bucket of income or fixed income or defensive assets, you're getting yields that there will be a whole host of people out there who have never experienced yields this high in their working career. Sort of multi-decade highs in Australian government bonds, in US treasuries, in other developed market government bonds. And that means the oil yield for really high quality credit is also pretty attractive. And and that hasn't been the case for several years. So for us remaining well exposed to that fixed income side, being thoughtful about getting yield and downside protection is is really important.

headline: Ascolum Capital has found value in emerging markets and specifically Asia over the past six months on attractive relative valuations and tech upside
reasoning: Poole says Ascolum has been building positions in emerging markets, particularly Asia, over the last six months. He cites materially better relative valuations compared to developed markets and upside from the tech thematic. He acknowledges some challenges from higher oil prices and growth, but sees the risk-reward as compelling. He describes it as a place where there is still material upside.
quote: Where we've found some value is in emerging markets and specifically Asia over the last six or so months. But relative valuations look very good. There are some challenges from higher oil prices and growth. But a bit more broadly, we saw it as a place where there was still some material upside from the story and the tech story. And those valuations just felt like a better place to be.

headline: Ascolum Capital expects hawkish holds to be common across developed market central banks through end of 2026
reasoning: Poole argued that inflation has impacted most of the world universally but growth impacts have been quite different by country. Central banks want to support growth but cannot afford to let inflation get out of hand. The hurdle for central banks to hike is elevated across Europe, Australia and the US. He suspects policy rates across the developed world will look very similar to current levels at year end, making hawkish holds the most likely outcome.
quote: I think the challenge central banks around the world are facing is that inflation has impacted most parts of the world universally. But the growth impact has been quite different. And the UK is a good example of this where inflation is above what I would like to be, although a little lower than consensus expected this month. But the growth is being impacted. So hawkish holds are perhaps going to be more common. I think the hurdle for central banks to hike or many central banks to hike at the moment is elevated. That's true in Europe going forward. I think it's true here in Australia and also true in the US where there's a little bit of tough talk there. But overall, I suspect interest rates or policy rates across the developed world would look very similar to what they look like now at the end of this year.

headline: Ascolum Capital sees current moment as good opportunity to pick up yield in government bonds with potential for solid capital gains over next six months

headline: Ascolum Capital is cautiously and selectively underweight Australian equities due to underwhelming growth outlook and commodity/bank concentration

headline: Ascolum Capital has US equity exposure but is cautious given stretched valuations requiring solid earnings growth to justify
